stem: A hospital wants to sample patient discharges and is sure that the three wards discharge patients differently. It takes a random sample from each ward separately. Which sampling method is this?
options: Simple random sampling
Convenience sampling
Systematic sampling
Stratified sampling
explanation: Dividing the population into groups (strata) expected to differ and sampling randomly within each is stratified sampling. It guarantees every ward is represented and lets the wards be compared (Day 6).
distractor_notes: Simple random sampling would draw from all discharges together, and could under-represent a small ward.
Convenience sampling takes whatever is easiest, and is not a valid method.
Systematic sampling takes every k-th unit.

stem: To estimate the error rate in last month's 3,000 invoices, a clerk checks the 100 invoices that customers have already queried. What is wrong with this sample?
options: It is biased: queried invoices are more likely to contain errors, so the estimate will be too high
It is too small: a proportion needs at least 500 observations
It is stratified: only one stratum (queried invoices) was sampled, which is acceptable
It is systematic: every 30th invoice was checked, so periodic errors are missed
explanation: The invoices were selected because something was already wrong with them, so they do not represent the 3 000. That is sampling bias from convenience sampling. Taking more queried invoices would not help; the selection method must change to random or stratified (Day 6).
distractor_notes: Size is not the main problem; even a large biased sample is wrong.
One self-selected group is not a stratum; the sample is convenience-based and biased.
Nothing was taken at a fixed interval.

stem: A bottling line has 12 filling heads that fill in rotation. A technician samples every 12th bottle for weight. What is the risk with this plan?
options: The sample will contain too many bottles from the fastest head
Every sampled bottle comes from the same filling head, so the other 11 heads are never checked
The sample will be too small to estimate the mean weight
The sample will over-represent the last bottles of each shift
explanation: Systematic sampling fails when the process has a cycle that matches the sampling interval (periodicity). Every 12th bottle here is always from one head. Using an interval that does not divide the cycle, or random sampling, avoids it (Day 6).
distractor_notes: Every 12th bottle is always the same head, not the fastest one.
Sample size is unrelated to the interval problem.
The interval matches the head cycle, not the shift.

stem: A sample was taken by convenience and is known to be unrepresentative. Which of the following would fix the problem?
options: Selecting the units by a proper random or stratified method instead
Taking ten times as many units the same way
Reporting the median instead of the mean
Calculating the sample standard deviation with n − 1
explanation: Sampling bias is a property of the selection method. A bigger biased sample is still biased; only changing how units are chosen removes it. Statistical corrections operate on the numbers, not on who was chosen (Day 6).
distractor_notes: Size does not cure bias.
The median is robust to outliers, not to a biased sample.
The n − 1 divisor corrects the standard deviation estimate, not the selection.

stem: What defines a simple random sample?
options: Every k-th unit is selected after a random start
Units are chosen by an experienced inspector as typical of the process
Units are drawn from each subgroup in proportion to its size
Every unit has an equal chance of selection, made by a chance mechanism
explanation: Simple random sampling gives every unit an equal chance and uses random numbers or an equivalent chance device, not human choice. It needs a list of the population. Inspector choice is judgement sampling; every k-th is systematic; nearest is convenience (Day 6).
distractor_notes: That is systematic sampling.
That is judgement sampling, which reproduces the inspector's assumptions.
That is stratified sampling.

stem: A sample of 36 invoices has a standard deviation of 6.0 minutes. What is the standard error of the mean?
options: 1.00 minute
0.33 minutes
0.17 minutes
6.00 minutes
explanation: Standard error = s ÷ √n = 6.0 ÷ √36 = 6.0 ÷ 6 = 1.00 minute. Sample means scatter far less than individual invoices (Day 14).
distractor_notes: 0.33 divides by 18, a wrong square root.
0.17 divides by n (36) instead of √n.
6.00 is the standard deviation of individual values, not of the mean.

stem: What does the central limit theorem state?
options: Sample means are approximately normal with standard deviation σ ÷ √n, whatever the population's shape
Any sample of 30 or more values is itself normally distributed
The population mean equals the sample mean once n exceeds 30
Sample means have the same spread as individual values when n is large
explanation: The theorem is about the sampling distribution of the mean: its centre is μ, its spread is the standard error σ ÷ √n, and its shape approaches normal as n grows, regardless of the population's shape. It is why normal-based tools work on averages of non-normal data (Day 14).
distractor_notes: Individual values keep the population's shape; only their means become normal.
The sample mean estimates μ but does not equal it.
Means have a smaller spread, σ ÷ √n, than individual values.

stem: Repair times are strongly right-skewed. A Green Belt takes many samples of 40 repairs and plots the sample means. What shape will the plot of means have?
options: Bimodal, with short and long repairs separated
Right-skewed, like the individual repair times
Approximately normal, as the central limit theorem predicts for means
Left-skewed, as the averaging reverses the tail
explanation: With n = 40 the means of skewed data are close to normally distributed, centred on the population mean with spread σ ÷ √40. The individual repair times stay skewed; it is their averages that become normal (Day 14).
distractor_notes: Two peaks would need two mixed populations, not skew.
Skew in the individual values is largely averaged out in means of 40.
Averaging reduces skew; it does not reverse it.

stem: A sample of 36 invoices has a mean processing time of 42.0 minutes and a standard deviation of 6.0 minutes. Using a t critical value of 2.03, what is the upper limit of the 95% confidence interval for the mean?
options: 54.18 minutes
48.00 minutes
44.03 minutes
43.00 minutes
explanation: Standard error = 6 ÷ √36 = 1.0. Margin of error = 2.03 × 1.0 = 2.03. Upper limit = 42.0 + 2.03 = 44.03 minutes; the full interval is 39.97 to 44.03 (Day 14).
distractor_notes: 54.18 uses the standard deviation (6) instead of the standard error (1).
48.00 adds the standard deviation itself.
43.00 adds one standard error without the critical value.

stem: What is statistical inference?
options: Drawing conclusions about a population from a sample, with stated uncertainty
Displaying a data set on a histogram or box plot
Summarising a data set with its mean and standard deviation
Choosing the sampling method and sample size for a study
explanation: Descriptive statistics summarise the sample; inference goes further and says what the sample implies about the population, through confidence intervals and hypothesis tests, with the uncertainty stated (Day 14).
distractor_notes: Plotting is graphical analysis.
That is descriptive statistics.
Sampling design comes before inference.

stem: A 95% confidence interval for the mean fill weight is 249.2 g to 251.6 g. The target is 250 g. What can be concluded?
options: The process mean differs significantly from 250 g at α = 0.05
95% of individual bottles weigh between 249.2 g and 251.6 g
A mean of 250 g is consistent with the data; a two-tailed test at α = 0.05 would not reject
The process mean is exactly 250 g, since 250 lies inside the interval
explanation: The interval contains 250, so the data do not contradict a mean of 250. A confidence interval that includes the hypothesised value corresponds to a two-tailed test that fails to reject at the matching alpha. The interval is about the mean, not about individual bottles (Day 14).
distractor_notes: Significance would need the interval to exclude 250.
The interval describes where the population mean lies, not the spread of individual bottles.
The interval gives a range, not an exact value.

stem: The standard error of the mean for a sample of 36 (standard deviation 6.0) is 1.00. If the sample size is increased to 144, what is the new standard error?
explanation: Standard error = 6 ÷ √144 = 6 ÷ 12 = 0.50. Quadrupling the sample halves the standard error, because it depends on the square root of n (Day 14).
distractor_notes: 1.00 is the original standard error.
0.25 assumes the error falls in proportion to n; it falls with √n.
0.04 divides by n.

subtopic: General Concepts & Goals of Hypothesis Testing
stem: In a hypothesis test comparing two shifts' mean output, what does the null hypothesis state?
options: The difference is practically significant
The two shifts have the same mean output
Shift A has higher mean output than shift B
The two shifts have different mean output
explanation: The null hypothesis is always the statement of no effect or no difference: the means are equal. The alternative states the difference the test is trying to demonstrate (Day 14).
distractor_notes: Practical significance is judged separately from the test.
A directional claim is a one-tailed alternative.
A difference is the alternative hypothesis.

subtopic: General Concepts & Goals of Hypothesis Testing
stem: A test gives p = 0.31 with alpha = 0.05. Which is the correct statement of the conclusion?
options: Declare the test inconclusive, since p is between 0.05 and 0.50
Accept the null hypothesis, since the data show the means are equal
Fail to reject the null hypothesis, since the data do not show a difference
Reject the null hypothesis, since p is above alpha
explanation: p is above alpha, so H₀ is not rejected. The wording matters: the data have failed to show a difference, which is not proof that there is none, so H₀ is never "accepted" (Day 14).
distractor_notes: A clear non-significant result is a valid conclusion, not an error.
"Accept" claims proof of no difference, which a non-significant result cannot give.
Rejection needs p at or below alpha, not above it.

subtopic: General Concepts & Goals of Hypothesis Testing
stem: A hypothesis test returns p = 0.03. Alpha was set at 0.05. What is the decision?
options: Fail to reject the null hypothesis: the result is not significant
Raise alpha to 0.10 and repeat the test
Accept the alternative hypothesis with 97% certainty
Reject the null hypothesis: the result is significant at the 5% level
explanation: p ≤ α, so the null hypothesis is rejected and the result is significant at the 5% level. The p-value is not the probability that the alternative is true, and alpha is fixed before the test (Day 14).
distractor_notes: 0.03 is below 0.05, so H₀ is rejected.
Alpha is chosen before the data are seen and is not adjusted afterwards.
A p-value is not the probability that either hypothesis is true.

subtopic: General Concepts & Goals of Hypothesis Testing
stem: What is a p-value?
options: The proportion of the sample that falls outside the specification limits
The probability that the alternative hypothesis is true, given the data
The probability that the null hypothesis is true, given the data
The probability of a result at least as extreme as the one observed, if the null hypothesis were true
explanation: The p-value measures how surprising the data would be under H₀. A small p-value means the data are unlikely if H₀ holds, so H₀ is rejected. It is not the probability of either hypothesis (Day 14).
distractor_notes: That is a defect proportion, unrelated to p-values.
Same error for the alternative.
The p-value is conditional on H₀ being true; it is not its probability.

stem: Comparing 5,000 invoices from each of two systems, the mean processing times are 40.2 and 40.0 minutes, p = 0.001. What should the Green Belt conclude?
options: The difference is statistically significant and practically important
The difference is practically important but not statistically significant
The difference is statistically significant but practically unimportant
The difference is neither statistically significant nor practically important
explanation: Very large samples detect tiny differences: p = 0.001 says the 0.2-minute gap is unlikely to be chance, not that it matters. Practical significance is judged from the effect size against the business case (Day 14).
distractor_notes: 0.2 minutes on a 40-minute process is not practically significant.
p = 0.001 is far below 0.05, so it is statistically significant.
It is statistically significant; it is the practical importance that is lacking.

stem: What is the difference between statistical significance and practical significance?
options: Statistical significance means the effect is large; practical significance means it is real
They are the same thing expressed in different units
Statistical significance means the effect is unlikely to be chance; practical significance means the effect is large enough to matter
Practical significance is measured by the p-value
explanation: A p-value addresses whether an effect could be chance. Whether the effect is worth acting on depends on its size and the business case, which the p-value does not measure. Both must be reported (Day 14).
distractor_notes: This reverses the two.
They answer different questions.
The p-value measures statistical significance only.

stem: A pilot compared 8 orders processed by a new method with 8 by the old. The new method averaged 12 minutes faster, but the test gave p = 0.14. The Champion says "so the new method makes no difference". What is the best response?
options: Disagree: with n = 8 the test has little power, so a real 12-minute gain could easily be missed
Agree, provided the data in both groups were normally distributed
Agree: a p-value above 0.05 shows the methods do not differ
Disagree: a 12-minute difference is always significant whatever the p-value
explanation: A non-significant result with a tiny sample usually means the test lacked power to detect the effect, not that the effect is absent. The 12-minute difference is practically important, so the right step is a larger sample (Day 14).
distractor_notes: Normality does not rescue the sample size problem.
Non-significance is not proof of no effect.
Significance depends on the p-value; the argument here is about power, not about the size alone.

stem: What is a Type I error?
options: Drawing a sample that is too small to detect the effect
Failing to reject a null hypothesis that is false
Rejecting a null hypothesis that is true
Using a one-tailed test where a two-tailed test was needed
explanation: A Type I error is a false alarm, and its probability is alpha. A Type II error is the reverse: missing an effect that is real, with probability beta (Day 14).
distractor_notes: Small samples raise beta (Type II risk), not Type I.
That is a Type II error.
That is a design mistake, not a Type I error.

stem: Alpha is set at 0.05. What does this value represent?
options: The probability computed from the sample data
The probability of failing to detect a real effect
The probability of rejecting a null hypothesis that is true
The probability that the test detects a real effect
explanation: Alpha is the significance level and equals the probability of a Type I error, a false alarm. Beta is the Type II risk and power is 1 − beta. The p-value is calculated from the data and compared with alpha (Day 14).
distractor_notes: The p-value comes from the data; alpha is chosen in advance.
The Type II error probability is beta.
Power is 1 − beta.

stem: A test has beta = 0.20. What is its power, and what does power mean?
options: 0.05: the probability of a Type I error
0.95: the confidence level
0.20: the probability of a false alarm
0.80: the probability of detecting an effect that really exists
explanation: Power = 1 − beta = 0.80: an 80% chance of rejecting H₀ when it is false. Power rises with larger samples, larger effects and higher alpha (Day 14).
distractor_notes: 0.05 would be alpha.
Confidence level is 1 − alpha, a different quantity.
0.20 is beta, the probability of missing a real effect.

stem: A team tested a new adhesive, concluded at p = 0.04 that it was stronger, and switched production to it. Six months later a larger study shows the two adhesives are equally strong. Which error did the team most likely make?
options: A Type I error: they rejected a true null hypothesis
A sampling bias: their sample was unrepresentative
A Type II error: they missed a real difference
A power error: their sample was too small to detect anything
explanation: The original test found an effect that later evidence shows was not real: a false alarm, which is a Type I error. With alpha = 0.05, one test in twenty on a true null hypothesis will do this by chance (Day 14).
distractor_notes: Nothing suggests the sample was unrepresentative; the result was chance at the 4% level.
A Type II error would be missing a real difference.
Low power causes missed effects, not false alarms.

stem: A team wants to know whether a new supplier's parts are stronger than the current supplier's parts. Which alternative hypothesis and test type are appropriate?
options: H₁: new mean > current mean; one-tailed
H₁: new mean = current mean; one-tailed
H₁: new mean < current mean; two-tailed
H₁: the means differ; two-tailed
explanation: The question has a direction (stronger), so the alternative is one-sided and the test is one-tailed, with all of alpha in the upper tail. The direction must be fixed before the data are examined (Day 14).
distractor_notes: Equality is the null hypothesis, not the alternative.
The direction is the wrong way, and a directional H₁ is one-tailed.
"Differ" would be two-tailed and is a weaker question than the one asked.

stem: A two-tailed test gives p = 0.053. If the same data are analysed with a one-tailed test in the direction of the observed difference, what is the p-value?
explanation: For the same data, the one-tailed p-value is half the two-tailed value: 0.053 ÷ 2 = 0.0265. That is why the tail must be chosen before seeing the data: switching afterwards turns a non-significant result into a significant one (Day 14).
distractor_notes: 0.053 is the two-tailed value unchanged.
0.106 doubles instead of halving.
0.0135 quarters it.

stem: Ten machines are measured for output before and after a maintenance change. Which type of test compares the before and after results?
options: A one-way ANOVA with before and after as two levels
A one-sample test of the after values against the before mean
A two-sample test treating before and after as independent groups
A paired test on the before-minus-after difference for each machine
explanation: The before and after readings come from the same machines, so the natural analysis is on the differences within each machine: a paired test. Treating them as two independent samples wastes the pairing and loses power (Day 14).
distractor_notes: ANOVA on two dependent groups has the same flaw as the two-sample test.
The before mean is not a fixed target; it is itself a sample.
The two sets are not independent; the same machines appear in both.

stem: A filling line is required to average 250 g. A sample of 30 bottles is weighed to check this. Which type of test is this?
options: A paired test comparing each bottle before and after filling
A one-sample test comparing the sample mean with the target of 250 g
A test of proportions on the share of bottles under 250 g
A two-sample test comparing this sample with last month's sample
explanation: One sample is compared with a fixed value, so it is a one-sample test (a one-sample t-test on Day 16). Two-sample and paired tests compare two sets of data; proportions apply to pass/fail data (Day 14).
distractor_notes: Nothing is measured twice on the same units.
Weight is continuous, not a proportion.
There is only one sample; the other side is a fixed target.

stem: For a one-tailed test at alpha = 0.05, what is the critical Z value?
explanation: With all 5% in one tail, the critical Z has 0.95 below it: 1.645. The two-tailed 5% value is 1.96 (2.5% in each tail); 2.576 is two-tailed 1%; 1.282 is one-tailed 10% (Day 14).
distractor_notes: 1.960 is the two-tailed 5% value.
2.576 is the two-tailed 1% value.
1.282 is the one-tailed 10% value.
